beats.caption: A CRM built for this demo — the host application
beats.say: Fine-grained access is already solved. You can scope a token to one project, or make it read-only. What nothing lets you do is grant it at the moment it's asked for, and have it expire on its own — permissions get arranged in advance, by somebody who isn't there when the work happens. This is a CRM, and this is the layer that does the other thing.

beats.caption: Selection proposes. It grants nothing.
beats.say: Selecting rows doesn't delegate them. What happens to be highlighted on your screen has no effect on what an assistant is able to do.

beats.caption: 2 accounts · 2 fields · 10 minutes
beats.say: This does. Two accounts, two fields, ten minutes, with a countdown that starts the moment it's granted.

beats.caption: document.modelContext.registerTool(...)
beats.say: Three things happen at once. The delegated rows are marked, the panel reads the scope back so a person can check what they just granted, and the browser registers a WebMCP tool that didn't exist a second ago — one that accepts only the records and the fields just chosen, and nothing wider.

beats.caption: executeTool(...) → staged, then OUT_OF_SCOPE
beats.say: The assistant calls that tool and a change appears against the record, staged but not saved. Then it asks for a record the permission never covered, and the call is rejected — not by the schema, by the server, which re-checks the mandate on every single request.

beats.caption: No apply tool. A person commits.
beats.say: And there is no apply tool. The inspector lists what was deliberately never registered, and applying is first on that list, so nothing on the assistant's side can commit. The person who granted the scope does it themselves.

beats.caption: The product: no panel, just the pill
beats.say: All of that panelling is instrumentation for the explanation. The real product has none of it — a badge that can't be hidden while a permission is live, and the decision shown on the record it affects.

beats.caption: Same layer, different host → mandate_stage_service_update
beats.say: And none of this knows what a CRM is. Same code, same server, a different application: a deployment console, where the records are services, the fields are replicas and feature flags, and the tool has renamed itself to match.

beats.caption: ChatGPT desktop · site tools · real executeTool calls
beats.say: None of that was staged, and this is not a mock-up: a real agent, in its own browser, working inside a permission granted a minute ago. Which is the shape people actually use. A colleague covering for you doesn't get your login — they get something small, decided on the spot, that lapses when you're back. That answer is already a permission. A mandate is only that answer, made into something software can hold.

beats.caption: Human intent, compiled into a live WebMCP contract
beats.say: A person's temporary intent, compiled into a live WebMCP contract and re-checked on every call. Next, that grant belongs in the agent's own chat window, where the asking already happens.
